title: Losing Power (E2, full, en)
text:
“Attention, students!” Ms. Johnson clapped her hands to get everyone’s attention. “We will be dismissing school early today”—Ms. Johnson paused as a ripple of excitement passed through the classroom—“because of the blizzard. We’ve called your parents and they should be picking you up shortly. Those students who ride the bus should head outside immediately.”

Karla stood up and quickly packed away her notebooks and pencils. She wanted to get one of the good seats on the bus and knew she had to hurry. Outside, it was pure chaos. The first snowflakes were already starting to fall and crowds of children waited to get on the bus. By the time Karla hopped off the bus at the end of her block, the snow was falling thickly. The ground was covered in white and the bus’s tires made black paths in the powder. Karla watched as new snowflakes quickly made the tracks disappear again.

When Karla walked through the front door, her parents were already home. They had been to the grocery store and stocked up on candles, water, milk, bread, and canned food for several days. Six years ago, there had been a blizzard, and her parents weren’t prepared. This time they wouldn’t make the same mistake. Karla couldn’t remember the last blizzard; she had only been three years old at the time.

“Why do we need candles, Dad?” Karla asked.

“Sometimes, the electricity goes out when there are blizzards. Snow builds up on power lines and all of that weight can cause a power line to break. Once a power line breaks, our electricity goes off. When this happens during a blizzard, it can take the electric company longer to fix the problem,” said her father.

“Because of the snow?” Karla asked.

“Exactly,” her dad nodded in approval. “The roads are often blocked so it’s harder for the trucks to make it to the broken power lines.”

They switched on the television to watch the news. The weather forecast said that it was going to snow for another twelve hours. Karla smiled. If it snowed for twelve more hours, she would definitely not have school the next day.

Karla spent the rest of the afternoon building a snowman and participating in the neighborhood snowball fight. When she came in for dinner, her cheeks were red from the cold. The house felt warm and toasty. Karla decided that she liked blizzards. Karla had just bitten into her enchiladas when all of a sudden the power went out. The house was plunged into total darkness.

“Karla?” her mother said. “Are you okay? I’m going to get some candles.” A moment later a light flickered as her mother set a candle in the middle of the table. Karla thought the shadows that the candlelight cast on her parents’ faces made it look like they were about to tell ghost stories. The darkness suddenly seemed a little bit scary. Her father went outside and came back to report that the entire neighborhood didn’t have power. It looked like the power wouldn’t come back on that night.

“Will the heat go off?” Karla asked her dad. “Will we be able to use the water?”

“Don’t worry, sweetie,” said her father. “The heat and the water are both still on.”

Karla looked at him, confused. How could the heat and the water work if all of the electricity didn’t work? “Come with me,” her father said. “I’ll show you in the basement.”

In the basement was a big metal tank with pipes coming out of it. “That’s the boiler,” said her father. “Our heat runs on gas, not electricity. As long as the gas pipes don’t break, we’ll still have heat. The water is the same way. It runs through pipes in the ground and as long as those pipes don’t freeze, we’ll be able to have running water.”

Karla thought about this. “So there are three different systems in our house?” she asked. Her father nodded. “Cool!” she said.

They went back upstairs and finished dinner. Afterwards, Karla and her mom made s’mores by melting marshmallows over candle flames. When Karla went to sleep that night, she felt lucky. It was cold and snowing outside but she had a warm bed to sleep in.
